A Preview of Kansas City’s 2026–2027 Arts Season

by Evan Pagano
0 0
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 18:33
Instaread

In Kansas City, activity picks up in the fall—and, tried and true, the arts emerge as an escape from it all. The 2026–2027 arts season offers a wealth of choices for art connoisseurs and casual admirers alike. Consider this your handy guide.

Museums & Exhibits

The Arts Council of Johnson County

The Arts Council of Johnson County awards scholarships, plans inclusive programs, and generally bolsters the JoCo arts scene. Every year it collaborates with the Lenexa Arts Council to organize Place of Peace (Oct. 27–Nov. 29), an exhibition of work by local veterans at the Lenexa City Hall Art Gallery. It also supports local galleries, including the Tim Murphy Art Gallery, whose monthly exhibitions spotlight local and regional artists. Pour and Pencil, for example, includes the works of local architect Bradford Athey (Aug. 6–29)

Charlotte Street

Since 1997, Charlotte Street has fueled Kansas City’s arts scene with grants, residencies, and platforms—and it just keeps pumping. Its upcoming multidisciplinary exhibition Digital Prairie (Aug. 15–Sept. 23) will explore the parallels and intersections of technology and ecology on the American prairie. Other fall highlights include two free film festivals—KC Underground Film Festival (Sept. 11/12, 17–19) and Nightshades Experimental Animation Festival (Nov. 13/14)—as well as September and October refreshes of the Crossroads ArtBoards above 125 Southwest Boulevard. 

Johnson County Arts & Heritage Center

Johnson County Arts & Heritage Center is an artistic marvel in itself, with its futurist architecture making it one of the county’s most recognizable buildings. It houses, among other things, the Johnson County Museum, a black box theater, and an art gallery. Patterns of The Prairie, a collection of works dedicated to these understated ecosystems, is on display in the gallery until Aug. 15. Everyday Democracy: Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness in Johnson County runs in the Johnson County Museum through Jan. 9. 

Kansas City Artists Coalition

Kansas City Artists Coalition is a nonprofit engine for innovation and amplification of visual arts. Every year, its galleries host artists from an array of disciplines, and this season stretches that ambition further. Cross Threaded, an eclectic collection of textile art, is on view until Sept. 4. The multisensory exhibition Edge Effect, running Sept. 18–Nov. 6, examines the messy intersection of rural and urban environments. During that same time frame, The Distance Between by Matthew Willie Garcia transforms the Snap Space Gallery with printed matter, projection mapping, and sculpture.

Kansas City Public Library

Beyond the books, Kansas City’s libraries are stacked—pun intended—with art and special exhibitions. At the downtown Central Library, three exhibitions full of historical photography are on view. A People’s History of Kansas City Soccer! through Oct. 4, Detoured: The Making of Bruce R. Watkins Drive through Dec. 31, and Hell and High Water: The 1951 Kansas City Flood through Jan. 3.

Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art

For over three decades, the Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art has provided a platform for emerging, mid-career, and established artists, and its temporary exhibitions routinely enliven the KC arts scene. Second Nature: Photography in the Age of the Anthropocene, a pictorial meditation on the human-centered planet, remains on view until Sept. 13. Lie. Sit. Stand. Be Still. (Aug. 28–Jan. 31) will depict, and encourage, moments of pause and rest through figurative works, abstractions, and other imagery. Barbara Takenaga: Awestruck (Oct. 6–April 11) will survey Takenaga’s grand abstractions over the last 25 years.

The Museum of Kansas City

The Museum of Kansas City is a Beaux-Arts beauty in Northeast Kansas City that houses a massive collection of artifacts and art. Until Jan. 10, you can view Connecting Cultures Across Kansas City, an exhibit of folk art, primarily from the American Southwest and Latin America. Through Feb. 21, the multidisciplinary Voices Now: Contemporary Native American Art spotlights living Indigenous American artists. And until June 27, Dunbar: Kansas City’s First Black Suburb gives voice to a culturally rich Kansas City neighborhood.

The National Museum of Toys and Miniatures

For certain eyes, there’s no place more mesmerizing than the National Museum of Toys and Miniatures. On the first floor, you’ll see everyday items and places miniaturized and rendered in near one-to-one detail; on the second, you’ll find pristine historic toys from a collection of over 65,000. Through Jan. 25, experience Native Arts in Miniature, which explores the diverse tribal traditions and creative innovations of Native American artists working in miniature. Art of the Imagination Case, a collection of miniature paintings and more by Kansas City artist Coti Meyer, is on view through April 19.

The National WWI Museum & Memorial

This towering Kansas City icon goes deep into the human stories and societal ripples of the Great War. In addition to its incomparable permanent galleries, The National WWI Museum & Memorial hosts several special exhibitions, each peeling back new layers of the conflict. Paris at War depicts a thriving French capital faced with war at its door. The Beautiful Game shows soccer’s surprising relationship with WWI. In the basement, the ever-changing Bergman Family Gallery and Open Storage Center lets guests peer in on artifacts being catalogued and preserved.

The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art

Kansas City’s seat of visual art is, as always, presenting coveted artwork from across eras and regions. Last April, The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art showcased Timeless Mucha—a popular exhibition of Art Nouveau works by French illustrator Alphonse Mucha—began a run that ends on Aug. 31. Elsewhere in the Bloch Building, American Prospects and Landscape Photography, 1839 to Today (Oct. 3–Jan. 3) will survey the history of American landscapes with an anchor in Joel Sternfeld’s influential 1980s work. In Gallery 214, Out of Many, One (Aug. 1–Jan. 17), which exhibits series from the Lawrence Lithography Workshop.

Nerman Museum of Contemporary Art

The Nerman’s eye-catching minimalist architecture and year-round galleries are enough to draw 100,000 visitors every year, and its special exhibitions keep it fresh. A duo of soccer-focused exhibitions—Sport and Spectator and Betsabeé Romero’s A Field with Roots (Un campo con raíces)—will remain on view until Dec. 6, as will the incisive works of Carlos Rolón and Norman Akers. Amy Kligman’s heralded interactive installation The Salon for Possible Futures concludes its extended stay on Dec. 22.

Performing Arts

1900 Building

Mission Woods’ stunning 1900 Building rounds out 2026 with a varied musical lineup. On Aug. 14, vocalist Sara Prince and pianist Anthony T. Edwards team up for Take Note Cabaret, a benefit for the disability-inclusive Spinning Tree Theatre. On Sept. 23, the prolific Italian singer and flatpicking guitarist Beppe Gambetta performs. Compositions & Reflections pairs Pan American pianist Carolina Calvache with Ensemble Ibérica’s Emerging Artists Collaborative on Nov. 7, and Nov. 12 brings the quick-fingered flutist/fiddler duo of Chris Norman and David Greenberg.

Bach Aria Soloists

The Bach Aria Soloists—a violin-keyboard-soprano trio specializing in classical compositions by Johann Sebastian Bach, his contemporaries, and his torchbearers—have stirred Kansas City audiences since 1999. In their 27th season, Kansas City Chorale veteran Lindsey Lang steps in as full-time soprano. It starts with a free concert at the Kemper (Sept. 19) and closes out autumn with their annual holiday concert at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church (Dec. 19).

City in Motion

For over 40 years, City in Motion has worked to make contemporary dance more accessible in Kansas City. They do it through education, public innovation, and the free Dance in the Park event each year. Attend the 27th annual event in Roanoke Park on Sept. 12.

Coterie Theatre

The Coterie Theatre, a resident of Crown Center, has served Kansas City’s families and young audiences for over 45 years. Its 2026–2027 season begins in spooky fashion with Electric Poe (Oct. 14–Nov. 1) at Union Cemetery. Back in Crown Center, The Pigeon Gets a Big Time Holiday Extravaganza! runs from Nov. 10 to New Year’s Eve. 

Folly Theater

The Folly Theater’s neon marquee beckons for a fall full of premium performances. In addition to hosting several of the organizations in this preview, the Folly boasts an original lineup of performances by the likes of cabaret legend Marilyn Maye (Sept. 15), bassist and composer Linda May Han Oh and her jazz group (Oct. 10), and singer and actress Bernadette Peters (Nov. 21). The Unauthorized Hallmark(ish) Parody Musical (Dec. 17) will end fall with a laugh.

The Friends of Chamber Music

What started in 1975 as a series of concerts in private homes is now a mainstay at revered KC venues. The Friends of Chamber Music‘s 51st season opens at the Folly on Sept. 19 with American Landscapes, consisting of compositions by Barber, Beach, and Dvořák. Then the rousing British vocal ensemble VOCES8 performs at Village Presbyterian Church in Prairie Village on Oct. 3, followed by the Modigliani string quartet at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Midtown (Oct. 16).

Harriman-Jewell Series

Since 1965, the Harriman-Jewell Series has brought the world’s best performing artists to Kansas City. Opera singer Luciano Pavarotti, cellist Yo-Yo Ma, and the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater have taken its stage. Its 62nd season begins Oct. 9 at the Folly Theater with cellist/pianist duo Alisa Weilerstein and Inon Barnatan. Other early shows include All The Devils Are Here (Nov. 5–6), actor Patrick Page’s one-man exploration of evil in Shakespeare’s works; and The Swingles: Together for the Holidays (Dec. 19).

Heartland Men’s Chorus

The beloved Heartland Men’s Chorus is entering its 41st season promoting pride, community, and expression in Kansas City. As usual, it all starts with a joyous holiday concert Dec. 4–6 at the Folly Theater.

Kansas City Actors Theatre

Kansas City Actors Theatre is celebrating its 22nd season as a vital outlet for actors in Kansas City. The three remaining productions have unique, gripping concepts: Intimate Apparel, featuring Chioma Anyanwu, (Aug. 5–23 at City Stage in Union Station) follows a seamstress in 1905 New York; Eureka Day (Sept. 9–27 at City Stage) looks in on Eureka Day School during a mumps outbreak; and Arms and the Man (Jan. 27–Feb. 14 at the Frantze Family Black Box Theatre) is a new adaptation of George Bernard Shaw’s 1894 comedy.

Kansas City Ballet

Kansas City Ballet, delighting fans of the art form since 1957, starts its 2026–2027 season on a fantastical note. First up is Septime Webre’s adaptation of The Wizard of Oz (Oct. 16–25). Next is the surreal Tchaikovsky classic, The Nutcracker (Nov. 28–Dec. 24), which includes a sensory-friendly rendition for neurodivergent spectators on Dec. 3. 

Kansas City Chorale

The Kansas City Chorale is an auditory marvel, with its 27 voices creating vibrant soundscapes at venues across KC. The 2026–2027 season begins Oct. 4/6 with Gretchaninoff’s Passion Week (in collaboration with another Kansas City choral group, Te Deum). This work is significant for the Kansas City Chorale—its 2007 recording of Passion Week earned the group its first of three Grammy Awards. 

Kansas City Jazz Orchestra

Kansas City Jazz Orchestra’s 2026–2027 Signature Series, Milestones, celebrates local and national jazz legends. The season begins with Spotlight: Charlie Parker on Aug. 29, followed by The Music of Miles Davis and John Coltrane on Nov. 7 and A Charlie Brown Christmas on Dec. 8. Its series of smaller shows, In My Jazz Era, consists of a quintet adaptation of Bruno Mars’s discography in September, a live score of Nosferatu on Halloween, and a holiday special at Tom’s Town Distilling Co. in December.

Kansas City Repertory Theatre

KCRep is a heavy hitter in the city’s theater scene, and its upcoming season starts strong with the Broadway hit Come From Away (Sept. 1–20), a touching musical about a Canadian town that took in rerouted airline passengers in the days after September 11. Another Broadway standout follows: John Proctor is the Villain, running Oct. 6–25. This season’s production of A Christmas Carol (Nov. 21–Dec. 24), a Kansas City tradition, will see Mark Robbins take over as Ebenezer Scrooge after Gary Neal Johnson’s 25-year run.

Kansas City Symphony

Matthias Pintscher’s third season as music director of the Kansas City Symphony is flush with diversity. The Classical Series kicks off with cellist Yo-Yo Ma on Sept. 30, then transitions to Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring Oct. 2–4. The Pops Series begins Oct. 16–18 with Dancing in the Street: The Music of Motown. Its list of special presentations is otherworldly: it includes the ambitious Prometheus (Sept. 9), Out of this World narrated by astronaut Col. Guy Gardner (Sept. 13), and a live score of the film Interstellar (Oct. 23–25). 

Kauffman Center Presents

The Kauffman Center for the Performing Arts regularly hosts local art powerhouses, but its Kauffman Center Presents series brings in artists from across the world. Just this fall, you can enjoy the vocal stylings of legendary Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant along with Saving Grace and Suzi Dian (Sept. 19), relive the music of the anime My Hero Academia (Oct. 6), spend an evening with the Irish singing group Celtic Thunder (Oct. 11), and experience world-class organist Anna Lapwood (Nov. 6)—all in the acoustic heaven that is Helzberg Hall.

KC Melting Pot Theatre

KC Melting Pot Theatre has been a bastion of Black theater in Kansas City for over a decade. Its 12th season—held exclusively in the Just Off Broadway Theatre in Penn Valley Park—opens Sept. 17–26 with August Wilson’s Jitney, a look inside an unregulated cab station facing erasure. Next up is a Dec. 3–12 run of the sitcom-esque Livin’ Fat, whose author, Judi Mason, has screenwriting credits that include Sanford and Son and Sister Act 2: Back in the Habit.

Lyric Opera KC

For seven decades, the Lyric Opera of Kansas City has adapted and thrived through fire, pandemic, and changing musical tastes. Its 70th season begins with a three-show run (Sept. 19, 25, and 27) of La bohème, the 1896 opera that inspired the 1996 musical Rent. Finishing fall is The Marriage of Figaro, composed by Mozart with a libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte (Nov. 7, 13, and 15).

Metropolitan Ensemble Theatre

Even fire couldn’t quell the artistic ambition of the Metropolitan Ensemble Theatre. When a 2024 blaze temporarily closed the Warwick Theatre, the company kept performing across KC. They’ll begin their second fall back at the Warwick with The Shark is Broken (Aug. 13–23), a behind-the-scenes look at the filming of Jaws. Next is part one of Angels in America, a Pulitzer-winning drama set during the AIDS crisis. And on the doorstep of winter, A Civil War Christmas: An American Musical Celebration will take place at the Alexander Majors Barn (Dec. 10–20). 

Midwest Trust Center

Johnson County Community College’s Midwest Trust Center has earned its reputation for a wide-ranging entertainment schedule. Its 2026–2027 season begins with three bangers: The Billy Joel Legacy (Oct. 11), rock opera The Who’s Tommy (Oct. 14), and Outlander in Concert (Oct. 23). Other fall highlights include multigenre father-son pianist duo Ryan & Ryan’s Kickin’ the Clouds Away (Oct. 25) and Take3’s Where Rock Meets Bach (Nov. 21).

Music Theater Heritage

Music Theater Heritage, one of Crown Center’s two in-house performing arts companies, packs its schedule with musical showcases. Two hot-ticket musicals remain this year—Jesus Christ Superstar (Aug. 20–Sept. 13) and Bat Boy, the Musical (Oct. 8–Nov. 1). The Ruby Room concert series runs year round, with tributes to Aretha Franklin (Sept. 16–20), Tom Petty and Bob Dylan (Nov. 4–8), and Christmas (Dec. 9–23) remaining in 2026.

New Theatre & Restaurant

Kansas City’s premier dinner theater makes for an unforgettable night out. Through Sept. 6, you can dine at the New Theatre & Restaurant and enjoy the Legally Blonde musical. Next on the menu is The Hallelujah Girls (Sept. 10–Nov. 15), starring Richard Karn of Home Improvement fame. Always… Patsy Cline, a musical play about the legendary country singer, runs Nov. 19 through January.

Owen/Cox Dance Group

The only thing predictable about the innovative Owen/Cox Dance Group is its schedule. Its 2026–2027 season includes two annual showcases—the free Creative Intersections in the Hyde Park Butterfly Garden (Aug. 7–8) and New Dance Partners at the Midwest Trust Center (Sept. 18–19)—plus a contemporary jazz adaptation of The Nutcracker and the Mouse King (Dec. 12–13) and Bach Moves (Feb. 13), a collaboration with the Bach Aria Soloists.

PNC Broadway in Kansas City

PNC Broadway in Kansas City splits its time between Kauffman Center for the Performing Arts and the Music Hall, and its lineups match that grandeur. The current season closes at the Music Hall August 12–30 with the heaviest of hitters: Wicked. The 2026–2027 season stays put Dec. 2–13 for another big swing, The Phantom of the Opera, before heading to the Kauffman Center for the Kansas City premiere of The Bodyguard—and five more premieres—in the new year.

Starlight Theatre

Everything feels bigger under the stars at Swope Park. Starlight Theatre—KCMO’s premier outdoor theater and concert venue—will conclude its 2026 AdventHealth Broadway series with the Monty Python “ripoff” Spamalot (Aug. 4–9), an in-house production of Newsies (Sept. 8–13), and the musical Beetlejuice (Oct. 2–4). Notable performers sprinkled in include Josh Groban (Sept. 1), Jerry Seinfeld (Sept. 18), and TLC and Salt-N-Pepa (Sept. 30).

Theatre in the Park

After ending its summer run in Shawnee Mission Park with The Hunchback of Notre Dame (Aug. 14–22), Theatre in the Park will close out its 2026 season in Johnson County Arts & Heritage Center’s black box theater. Dracula: A Comedy of Terrors (suited for ages 17 and up) ushers in Halloween time Oct. 3–8, and the family-friendly classic Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer runs Dec. 5–23.

UMKC Conservatory

Fall at the UMKC Conservatory—which teaches music, dance, and theater—is as packed as, well, a college curriculum. A handful of highlights: Sounding a Nation, a Conservatory Symphony Orchestra concert on Sept. 18; the inaugural Midwest Mariachi Festival in collaboration with the Sister Cities Association’s Guadalajara Committee on Sept. 26; three days of dance performances Oct. 3–5; and the return of Octubafest on Oct. 29 and 30. Theater performances will be announced as the semester advances.

Unicorn Theatre

The Unicorn Theatre isn’t playing it safe in its seven-show 53rd season. It opens with The Ritz (Aug 12–30), a comedy in which a straight man flees the mob to a predominantly gay bathhouse. Next is Red Like Fruit (Oct. 14–25), an award winner at Edinburgh Fringe that deals with domestic violence and traumatic memories. After that, Sherlock Holmes and the Adventure of the Elusive Ear (Nov. 11–29), with the perfect director for an idiosyncratic mystery: Sidonie Garrett, executive artistic director of the Heart of America Shakespeare Festival. The Unicorn is collaborating with Rainy Day Books to curate books related to each production.
